analysis.one_liner: Repeals the federal estate and gift tax on inherited wealth.
analysis.headline: The estate tax repeal bill died in the House Ways and Means Committee in 1998 without a vote and without a single cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would delete the estate and gift tax from the tax code, ending it for deaths and gifts after December 31, 2001. The estate tax applies only to the largest inherited fortunes, so its repeal would be a permanent tax cut for wealthy heirs, paid for by federal revenue everyone else relies on. The bill was referred to the tax-writing committee and never moved.
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs to the largest estates. The estate tax only applies above an exemption level, so repeal would cut taxes exclusively for families inheriting substantial wealth. Wealthy people making large lifetime gifts would also gain, since the gift tax would disappear with it.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the entire estate and gift tax subtitle of the tax code, effective for deaths and taxable gifts after December 31, 2001.
Because the estate tax is owed only by the largest estates, the benefit would flow almost entirely to heirs of significant wealth.

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury. Estate and gift tax revenue would disappear permanently, meaning the gap would have to be closed by higher other taxes, more borrowing, or cuts to programs funded by general revenue.

drawbacks.text: Repeal would permanently eliminate federal estate and gift tax revenue, shifting the cost onto other taxpayers or adding to the deficit.
The repeal would apply to all deaths and gifts after the effective date with no phaseout tied to estate size, so even the very largest fortunes would pay nothing.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit goes narrowly to heirs of the largest estates, while the cost — lost general revenue — is spread across everyone else. As written, the bill offers nothing in return for the revenue loss, making the trade strongly lopsided toward concentrated wealth.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and the Congress ended without any vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Joe Scarborough introduced the Estate Tax Sunset Act on May 13, 1998, to repeal the estate and gift tax.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day.
The committee took no further action, and the bill died when the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the federal Treasury kept estate and gift tax revenue that would otherwise have been permanently eliminated, and the largest estates continued to owe the tax.

for.name: Rep. Joe Scarborough
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the estate and gift tax.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on May 13, 1998 and took no action on it before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes and no cosponsors, so the record shows no evidence of support or opposition beyond the sponsor.

industries.industry: Heirs to large estates and wealthiest households
industries.note: Repeal would eliminate the tax on the largest inherited fortunes and on large lifetime gifts. The cost would fall on general federal revenue rather than on any offsetting group.

Lawyers, accountants, and advisors who sell estate planning services partly because of the estate tax would lose that business. Their interest is not directly against the public, but repeal would end the problem they are paid to manage.
Permanent elimination of estate and gift tax revenue would leave other taxpayers or federal programs to absorb the loss.
